stories.headline: Trump envoy Witkoff meets Putin in St Petersburg for Ukraine war talks
stories.title: Trump envoy Witkoff meets Putin in St Petersburg for Ukraine war talks
stories.summary: Moscow, Oct 21: US envoy Steve Witkoff held talks with Russian President Vladimir Putin in St Petersburg on Wednesday about Moscow's full-scale invasion of Ukraine, as US President Donald Trump pushes Kyiv to make a deal that stops the fighting. Witkoff said in televised remarks at the start of the meeting that he hoped to discuss the resumption of the trilateral talks involving the US, Russia and Ukraine that would allow the technical teams to discuss the next steps toward a peace settlement. Putin thanked Trump and Witkoff for their efforts to end the war. The visit came a day after Witkoff met with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy and some European leaders in the Norwegian capital, Oslo. Witkoff's meetings suggested leaders are keen to bring new momentum to US-led peace efforts, more than 4 ½ years after Russia's army invaded. Efforts by the Trump administration since early last year to end the war have made no significant progress, and there was no suggestion of an imminent breakthrough. Russia and Ukraine are still far apart in their terms for a settlement, as their armies remain locked on the battlefield and they pummel each other with daily long-range strikes. However, Finnish President Alexander Stubb said late Tuesday that the Oslo meeting, which he attended, “made genuine progress.” Witkoff sees some degree of momentum' in peace efforts Witkoff and Putin met at St Petersburg's Constantine Palace, with Russian presidential envoy Kirill Dmitriev and Putin's foreign affairs adviser Yuri Ushakov also at the table. Witkoff said Trump's son-in-law Jared Kushner would join the discussion via a video link. Witkoff said he would inform Putin about Tuesday's talks in Oslo, which he described as “productive,” adding that “there is some degree of momentum.” He thanked Putin for lifting Russia's ban on diesel exports, which angered some US lawmakers, adding that it would help reduce prices for US farmers and truckers. Putin said he was ready to discuss prospects for the restoration of US-Russian economic ties, adding that he is also prepared to discuss the US-led conflict with Iran. Moscow is ready to use its special relationship with Tehran to help bring peace, he said. Putin was also due to meet Wednesday with Chinese Premier Li Qiang, who was in St Petersburg meeting with other Russian top officials, the Kremlin said. Russia has cultivated its ties with China, and the two countries last month vetoed a US proposal for UN experts to keep monitoring sanctions on Iran. Norway's prime minister sees a possible new phase' in talks Witkoff planned to return to Oslo for more consultations after his trip to Russia, Norwegian Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Støre said. “I think we may have entered a phase now where the Russians are also looking for opportunities for diplomacy,” Støre told Norwegian broadcaster NRK on Wednesday morning. Zelenskyy was still in Oslo on Wednesday, where he was visiting the country's Parliament and meeting lawmakers. Witkoff appeared to be making another attempt at overcoming hurdles that have kept a deal out of reach. Zelenskyy said Tuesday that on the agenda were future security guarantees for Ukraine, the fate of occupied territories, postwar reconstruction, and the possibility of a ceasefire. Trump said Oct. 11 that Russia and Ukraine had agreed to a ceasefire in attacks on energy infrastructure but Russia has kept hammering Ukraine's power grid and Kyiv has hit Russian oil refineries. Ukrainian strikes set an oil export terminal and a depot ablaze in St. Petersburg on Sunday as Kyiv launched more than 1,000 drones at Russia in one of its largest aerial attacks of the war. Trump presses Zelenskyy to compromise Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov said Tuesday that Moscow is willing to listen to new US proposals about Ukraine but he doesn't expect any “miracle” from Washington. At the White House on Tuesday, Trump increased the pressure on Zelenskyy to come to an agreement with Russia as relations between the two men have soured again. “We want Zelenskyy to make a deal,” Trump told reporters in the Oval Office. “We've given a lot to Ukraine. We've gotten absolutely nothing back except grief, death, tremendous monetary loss.” If that doesn't happen, “I think it's going to be a very bad thing,” Trump said. Amid fears that Washington was turning its back on Ukraine, Zelenskyy said Kyiv is once again receiving early warnings from its partners about incoming Russian missiles, after recent strikes that he said occurred without enough notice from allies. The change happened after Zelenskyy spoke with his American counterparts, including a phone call with US Secretary of State Marco Rubio. Russian attacks kill 5 people and injure 25 others, Ukraine says Overnight Russian attacks in Kyiv left three people dead and 12 injured, while 10 residential buildings were damaged, the city's military administration said. Energy facilities were targeted in Kyiv and three other cities in Russian attacks early Wednesday, Ukrainian Prime Minister Serhii Koretskyi said. Outside the eastern city of Kharkiv, two people died and 11 were wounded when drones exploded in a residential area, he said. The Russian Defence Ministry said that its forces overnight struck a warehouse, an electrical substation and a bulk carrier at sea that was headed to the Ukrainian port of Odesa. The Russian Defence Ministry reported Wednesday that its air defences overnight intercepted 373 Ukrainian drones over multiple Russian regions, as well as illegally annexed Crimea and the Black Sea. (AP)

stories.headline: Vikramaditya Singh seeks paper ballots, Election Commission reforms
stories.title: Vikramaditya Singh seeks paper ballots, Election Commission reforms
stories.summary: Vikramaditya Singh seeks paper ballots, Election Commission reforms
reasons: corroboration: single independent source -> medium confidence
article_sentences: Vikramaditya Singh called for paper-ballot elections and reforms within the Election Commission.
The demand intensifies opposition pressure over EVMs, voter-roll revisions and democratic safeguards.

Himachal Pradesh Public Works Department Minister Vikramaditya Singh on Wednesday called for elections to be conducted using paper ballots instead of electronic voting machines and sought reforms within the Election Commission to protect democracy and the Constitution, news agency Press Trust of India reported.
Singh also reiterated the opposition's demands for the resignation of Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar and the withdrawal of legal immunity granted to Election Commissioners.
Addressing a press conference in Shimla, Singh said the opposition and the public had placed their trust in the Supreme Court.
He stressed that necessary reforms must be introduced to strengthen the democratic system and protect the Constitution.
He was referring to a petition filed in the Supreme Court by members of the INDIA bloc challenging the Special Intensive Revision of electoral rolls and alleged deletion of voters' names.
Singh described the action against opposition leaders and protesters in Delhi as unfortunate, saying the national capital had been turned into “something resembling a military cantonment”.
The Congress MLA expressed concern over the deployment of paramilitary forces and the detention of people.
He alleged that people were being detained at their homes and airports, with some even being held on board aircraft, in an apparent reference to CJP founder Abhijeet Dipke, PTI reported.
Dipke was detained inside an Air India flight shortly after it landed at Delhi airport on October 10 to prevent him from participating in a CJP protest against Kumar.
Singh said the opposition would continue its struggle to protect democratic rights and the Constitution.

stories.headline: India and the digital quarter-century
stories.title: India and the digital quarter-century
stories.summary: At my first posting in 1977, banking meant handwritten scrolls, ledgers and sheets of carbon paper. I wrote so much that I developed corn on my finger. Today, a street vendor can receive a QR-code payment before the customer has put away the phone. Few contrasts capture India’s transformation more vividly.This is not principally a banking story. It is the story of how a country once defined by scarcity, distance and administrative complexity began using technology to turn scale into economic strength.From a Large Economy to a Connected OneIn 2000, India’s gross domestic product was about $468 billion. By 2025, it had risen to nearly $3.96 trillion in current-dollar terms, according to the World Bank data. At the end of 2025, India also had more than one billion broadband subscriptions, according to TRAI (Telecom Regulatory Authority of India).Connectivity has reduced the cost of distance. A small enterprise can reach customers nationally without first building a national physical network; a migrant worker can transfer money home instantly; and an entrepreneur can begin with cloud software rather than heavy infrastructure. By December 2025, India had more than 2.07 lakh recognised startups, which reported creating over 21.9 lakh direct jobs, according to DPIIT (Department of Promotion of Industry and Internal Trade).The business environment remains a work in progress. Digitising a complicated process does not automatically make it simple. Yet online systems for taxation, company filings, procurement and enterprise registration have widened participation in the formal economy and made markets more accessible.Also Read: 25 years of Prime Minister Narendra Modi in public office: Shaping governanceGovernment as a Builder of Digital RailsThe government’s most consequential role has not been to create every digital service. It has been to establish identity, payment and data rails on which public institutions and private businesses can build.Aadhaar, Jan Dhan, mobile connectivity, UPI and Direct Benefit Transfer (DBT) emerged through coordination among government, regulators, banks, the National Payments Corporation of India (NPCI), technology companies and frontline workers. Policy continuity mattered, as did the preference for interoperable infrastructure rather than isolated, closed systems.The scale is remarkable. As of August 5, the Jan Dhan programme had 58.97 crore beneficiaries; 32.86 crore were women and 45.86 crore were served through rural and semi-urban branches. In FY24–25, UPI processed 185.9 billion transactions worth about ₹260.6 lakh crore. The DBT platform reports cumulative transfers of nearly ₹52.96 lakh crore.These figures illustrate a distinctive Indian model. Government helped build common rails and established trust; banks, fintechs, businesses and millions of citizens converted them into everyday utility. The result has been a large, low-cost arena for innovation.Reaching the Last MileMy years in banking gave me a front-row seat to this transition, but they also taught me not to confuse a digital launch with a social outcome. An account opened is not necessarily an account used. An application is not inclusive if the customer lacks connectivity, confidence, language support or a reliable way to resolve a problem.In branches and rural communities, I saw that technology worked best when paired with human assistance—business correspondents, self-help groups, trained employees and trusted local institutions. Digital infrastructure should not simply remove people from processes. It should free people from routine work so they can focus on advice, credit, enterprise and problem-solving.That is why grassroots adoption remains central. India’s next phase must invest in digital literacy, accessible design and assisted channels, particularly for women, small farmers, micro-enterprises, older citizens and first-time users.Also Read: Unleashing India's potential over 25 yearsCovid-19: A National Stress TestCovid-19 caused enormous human and economic suffering, but it also revealed the value of India’s digital foundations. Payments, benefit transfers, remote work, online commerce and digital public services became instruments of continuity almost overnight.I had earlier tried to introduce a work-from-home option in banking, especially for employees managing care responsibilities. It encountered resistance because physical presence was often confused with productivity. The pandemic overturned that assumption. When I moved into enterprise technology in 2020, I watched organisations compress years of digital change into months.At the national level, CoWIN provided scheduling, stock tracking and verifiable certificates for a vaccination programme that had administered more than 220 crore doses by January 2023. India also offered the platform as an open-source digital public good to other countries. It showed that software built for Indian scale could have global relevance.From Indian Innovation to a Global ReferenceIndia’s digital public infrastructure is now studied internationally because it offers a model in which the state creates foundational, interoperable systems and public and private providers innovate above them.A G20 report developed with the World Bank observed that India moved transaction-account ownership from roughly one-fourth of adults in 2008 to more than 80 percent—a journey estimated to have taken as long as 47 years without digital public infrastructure.India’s global contribution is, therefore, larger than any single platform. It is the demonstration that population-scale systems can be designed as shared infrastructure. The corresponding responsibility is to ensure that openness and speed are matched by cybersecurity, privacy, consumer protection and accountable governance. Women form the majority in all of Jan Dhan accounts. And SBI holds a major share of all Jan Dhan accounts in India, managing tens of millions of these accounts. Photo by Idrees Mohammed / AFPTurning Access into AgencyThe past 25 years have changed my understanding of technology. I once saw it largely as a means of automating processes. I now see it as an operating system for economic participation.The next wave—powered by artificial intelligence, trusted data and automation—could make Indian businesses more productive and globally competitive. But durable value will require organisations to redesign work, develop skills and retain human judgement. The government must continue to provide enabling infrastructure and clear rules, while enterprise competes, innovates and invests responsibly.India has built an extraordinary infrastructure of access. The test of the next 25 years is whether that access becomes agency: Whether a farmer receives timely credit, a woman entrepreneur reaches a national market, a small business uses AI productively, and every citizen can participate in growth with dignity. That is when digital transformation becomes national transformation.

opening: At my first posting in 1977, banking meant handwritten scrolls, ledgers and sheets of carbon paper.
I wrote so much that I developed corn on my finger.
body: Today, a street vendor can receive a QR-code payment before the customer has put away the phone.
Few contrasts capture India’s transformation more vividly.
This is not principally a banking story.
It is the story of how a country once defined by scarcity, distance and administrative complexity began using technology to turn scale into economic strength.
From a Large Economy to a Connected.
In 2000, India’s gross domestic product was about $468 billion.
By 2025, it had risen to nearly $3.96 trillion in current-dollar terms, according to the World Bank data.
At the end of 2025, India also had more than one billion broadband subscriptions, according to TRAI (Telecom Regulatory Authority of India).
Connectivity has reduced the cost of distance.

A small enterprise can reach customers nationally without first building a national physical network; a migrant worker can transfer money home instantly; and an entrepreneur can begin with cloud software rather than heavy infrastructure.
By December 2025, India had more than 2.07 lakh recognised startups, which reported creating over 21.9 lakh direct jobs, according to DPIIT (Department of Promotion of Industry and Internal Trade).
The business environment remains a work in progress.
Digitising a complicated process does not automatically make it simple.
Yet online systems for taxation, company filings, procurement and enterprise registration have widened participation in the formal economy and made markets more accessible.
Government as a Builder of Digital Rails.
The government’s most consequential role has not been to create every digital service.
It has been to establish identity, payment and data rails on which public institutions and private businesses can build.

Aadhaar, Jan Dhan, mobile connectivity, UPI and Direct Benefit Transfer (DBT) emerged through coordination among government, regulators, banks, the National Payments Corporation of India (NPCI), technology companies and frontline workers.
Policy continuity mattered, as did the preference for interoperable infrastructure rather than isolated, closed systems.
The scale is remarkable.
As of August 5, the Jan Dhan programme had 58.97 crore beneficiaries; 32.86 crore were women and 45.86 crore were served through rural and semi-urban branches.
In FY24–25, UPI processed 185.9 billion transactions worth about ₹260.6 lakh crore.
The DBT platform reports cumulative transfers of nearly ₹52.96 lakh crore.
These figures illustrate a distinctive Indian model.
Government helped build common rails and established trust; banks, fintechs, businesses and millions of citizens converted them into everyday utility.
The result has been a large, low-cost arena for innovation.
Reaching the Last MileMy years in banking gave me a front-row seat to this transition, but they also taught me not to confuse a digital launch with a social outcome.
An account opened is not necessarily an account used.
An application is not inclusive if the customer lacks connectivity, confidence, language support or a reliable way to resolve a problem.
In branches and rural communities, I saw that technology worked best when paired with human assistance—business correspondents, self-help groups, trained employees and trusted local institutions.
Digital infrastructure should not simply remove people from processes.
It should free people from routine work so they can focus on advice, credit, enterprise and problem-solving.
That is why grassroots adoption remains central.
India’s next phase must invest in digital literacy, accessible design and assisted channels, particularly for women, small farmers, micro-enterprises, older citizens and first-time users.
Covid-19: A National Stress TestCovid-19 caused enormous human and economic suffering, but it also revealed the value of India’s digital foundations.
Payments, benefit transfers, remote work, online commerce and digital public services became instruments of continuity almost overnight.
I had earlier tried to introduce a work-from-home option in banking, especially for employees managing care responsibilities.
It encountered resistance because physical presence was often confused with productivity.
The pandemic overturned that assumption.
When I moved into enterprise technology in 2020, I watched organisations compress years of digital change into months.
At the national level, CoWIN provided scheduling, stock tracking and verifiable certificates for a vaccination programme that had administered more than 220 crore doses by January 2023.
India also offered the platform as an open-source digital public good to other countries.
It showed that software built for Indian scale could have global relevance.
From Indian Innovation to a Global Reference.

India’s digital public infrastructure is now studied internationally because it offers a model in which the state creates foundational, interoperable systems and public and private providers innovate above them.

A G20 report developed with the World Bank observed that India moved transaction-account ownership from roughly one-fourth of adults in 2008 to more than 80 percent—a journey estimated to have taken as long as 47 years without digital public infrastructure.
India’s global contribution is, therefore, larger than any single platform.
It is the demonstration that population-scale systems can be designed as shared infrastructure.
The corresponding responsibility is to ensure that openness and speed are matched by cybersecurity, privacy, consumer protection and accountable governance.
Women form the majority in all of Jan Dhan accounts.
And SBI holds a major share of all Jan Dhan accounts in India, managing tens of millions of these accounts.
Photo by Idrees Mohammed / AFPTurning Access into Agency.
The past 25 years have changed my understanding of technology.
I once saw it largely as a means of automating processes.
I now see it as an operating system for economic participation.
The next wave—powered by artificial intelligence, trusted data and automation—could make Indian businesses more productive and globally competitive.
But durable value will require organisations to redesign work, develop skills and retain human judgement.
The government must continue to provide enabling infrastructure and clear rules, while enterprise competes, innovates and invests responsibly.
India has built an extraordinary infrastructure of access.

The test of the next 25 years is whether that access becomes agency: Whether a farmer receives timely credit, a woman entrepreneur reaches a national market, a small business uses AI productively, and every citizen can participate in growth with dignity.
That is when digital transformation becomes national transformation.

A G20 report developed with the World Bank observed that India moved transaction-account ownership from roughly one-fourth of adults in 2008 to more than 80 percent—a journey estimated to have taken as long as 47 years without digital public infrastructure.
And SBI holds a major share of all Jan Dhan accounts in India, managing tens of millions of these accounts.

stories.headline: Supreme Court judgment opens up the religion-neutrality of OBC classification for debate
stories.title: Supreme Court judgment opens up the religion-neutrality of OBC classification for debate
stories.summary: The Supreme Court clarifies that non-Hindu communities can be OBC, but distinguishes between the sources of backwardness for Hindu OBCs and non-Hindu OBCs on the question of continuing backwardness for converts
reasons: source: event has 2 copies, primary source counted once
corroboration: single independent source -> medium confidence
event term: 'supreme court' in title weight 44
event term: 'supreme court judgment' in title weight 46
event term: 'supreme court' in summary weight 26.4
article_sentences: The religion-neutrality of the Other Backward Classes (OBC) classification has been thrown open for debate after the Supreme Court’s recent decision that an OBC Hindu person loses the entitlement to reservation once they convert to another religion.

While the Scheduled Castes (SCs) have always been identified by a religion criterion, and the Scheduled Tribes (STs) classification has never considered religion, and the OBC classification, since its implementation after the 1992 Indra Sawhneyvs.
Union of India judgment, has remained religion-neutral.
Communities (whether classes or castes) are examined for 11 social, educational, and economic backwardness indicators, and then classified as such based on a threshold score.
Forms for OBC certificates across States do not ask for the religion of an applicant nor does an OBC certificate declare the holder’s religion.

In deciding the question of whether a Hindu OBC person is entitled to reservation after converting to another faith, the Supreme Court Bench of Justices Prashant Kumar Mishra and Shree Chandrashekhar, in its October 15 judgment, has established that the “source of social backwardness” must necessarily be considered in this inquiry.
The judgment noted that, for a Hindu OBC individual, the “legal foundation” of their entitlement to reservation is “specifically conditioned upon membership of that Hindu social order”.
Discussing the “source of social backwardness”, the court noted that while Indra Sawhneyvs.

Union of India prevented caste from being the sole criterion for OBC classification, what cannot be disregarded is that in Hindu society, the “foundational institution” of caste has historically determined social and other manifestations of backwardness.

While the court admitted in the judgment that educational, economic, and other forms of backwardness may continue for an OBC person who has left the Hindu faith, their very act of choosing another faith puts them in a different “social order”, altering the “source of social backwardness”, it has said.

This reading of the Bench of Justices Mishra and Chandrashekhar flows from how it has understood the idea of social stratification across faiths in India, essentially noting that the source of social backwardness varies based on the nature of social stratification in any given social order.

This understanding of social stratification makes a subtle departure from how the same concept was discussed in the Indra Sawhney judgment, which has laid the foundation for identifying OBCs so far, without entering the question of the source of social backwardness, regardless of whether the communities are classes or castes, Hindu or Muslim.

article_sentences: What are the two options proposed by SBI Research?
Under the first, conventional option, SBI Research proposes raising the repo rate by 50 bps from the current 5.50% to 6.00%.
Under this scenario, the marginal standing facility (MSF) rate would be 6.25%, while the standing deposit facility (SDF) rate would be 5.75%.
The second option combines a smaller repo rate increase with a change in the liquidity corridor.
Under this proposal, the repo rate would rise by 25 bps to 5.75%, while the MSF rate would be set at 6.25% and the SDF rate at 5.50%.
This would create an asymmetric LAF corridor, with a wider gap between the repo rate and the two standing facility rates.
SBI Research says such an approach could be considered amid global uncertainty and the need to maintain orderly market functioning.
How does the LAF corridor work?
The LAF corridor helps guide short-term money-market rates around the RBI's policy rate.
The repo rate is the rate at which banks borrow funds from the RBI against eligible securities.
The SDF allows banks to deposit surplus funds with the central bank, while the MSF enables eligible banks to obtain overnight liquidity at a rate above the repo rate.
Changes to these rates influence the cost and availability of short-term funds in the banking system.

article_sentences: The Supreme Court told the Andhra Pradesh poll panel to examine YSRCP complaints.
The directions underscore that secure nomination filing is integral to free and fair elections.
A vacation bench of Justices Joymalya Bagchi and V Mohana was hearing a petition filed by the Yuvajana Sramika Rythu Congress Party, or YSRCP.
The party alleged that violence and threats had prevented several of its candidates from filing nomination papers for elections to around 100 urban local bodies.

The bench directed the state election commission to consider complaints submitted by the YSRCP and other candidates, along with supporting material, and decide by Thursday whether to extend the nomination deadline.
It also asked the commission to take all necessary steps to address concerns among the YSRCP and other candidates about free and fair elections in the state.
The court directed the Andhra Pradesh Director General of Police to provide adequate security to candidates and election offices.
It observed that the filing of nomination papers was an essential part of free and fair elections.
The bench clarified that it was not directly intervening in the election process but was allowing the state election commission to consider the party's complaint and take an appropriate decision.
It asked the commission to file a compliance affidavit by October 27, the next date of hearing.
According to PTI, the court said the YS Jagan Mohan Reddy-led party had “made out prima facie case” that several of its candidates had been stopped from filing nomination papers.
The court referred to representations submitted by the party and its candidates, both physically and electronically, as well as video clips and other electronic evidence.
